title: The Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem
subject: Maths-2
description: Doubling and halving squares, √2 and its bounds, combining squares, the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras theorem, Baudhāyana triples, Fermat's Last Theorem and the lotus problem.

questions.question: Baudhāyana's Śulba-Sūtra, which asks how to construct a square of double the area, dates from about which time?
questions.explanation: The chapter dates Baudhāyana's Śulba-Sūtra to c. 800 BCE. Pythagoras came later (c. 500 BCE) and Euclid's Elements later still (c. 300 BCE).

questions.question: If every side of a square is doubled, the area of the new square becomes how many times the original area?
questions.explanation: Doubling both the length and the width multiplies the area by 2 × 2 = 4. That is why simply doubling the side does NOT give double the area.

questions.question: According to Śulba-Sūtra Verse 1.9, a square with double the area of a given square is built on which line segment?
options: one full side of the original square
half of one side of the original square
the diagonal of the original square
the perimeter of the original square
questions.explanation: Baudhāyana's verse says: 'The diagonal of a square produces a square of double the area of the original square.' The new square's side is the old square's diagonal.

questions.question: Why does the square built on the diagonal have exactly double the area of the original square?
options: the original is 4 small congruent triangles; the new one is 8 of them
the new square is two rectangles, each equal to the original square
the diagonal is exactly twice as long as a side of the square
the original is 2 small congruent triangles; the new one is 4 of them
questions.explanation: Drawing horizontal and vertical lines splits the original square into 2 congruent right triangles and the dotted square into 4 of the same triangles — 4 is double 2. The diagonal is not twice a side (it is √2 times).

questions.question: In the Śulba-Sūtra, Baudhāyana's 'east-west' and 'north-south' lines are best described as:
options: horizontal and vertical lines perpendicular to each other
the two diagonals of the square, crossing at its centre
lines drawn parallel to the diagonal of the square
compass directions marked only at the corners of an altar
questions.explanation: The text explains that east-west and north-south lines are horizontal and vertical lines that are perpendicular to each other — handy for cutting the squares into congruent triangles.

questions.question: Squares are built one on the diagonal of the previous; the first three contain 2, 4 and 8 small triangles. How many small triangles make up the 5th square in this sequence?
questions.explanation: Each square has double the area (and double the triangle count) of the previous one: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. The 5th square has 32 triangles; 16 is the 4th and 64 the 6th.

questions.question: A square has side 6 units. What is the area of the square constructed on its diagonal?
questions.explanation: The square on the diagonal has double the area: 2 × 36 = 72 sq units. 144 would be the area if the side were doubled; 48 confuses doubling the perimeter.

questions.question: Doubling the side of a square doubles its area.
questions.explanation: False. Doubling the side gives 2 × 2 = 4 times the area. To double the area you must build the new square on the diagonal.

questions.question: In the doubling construction, each side of the original square bisects an angle of the new dotted square.
questions.explanation: True. The hint notes that the vertical and horizontal sides of the original square bisect the angles of the dotted square, which is why extending them passes through its vertices.

questions.question: Select ALL the correct statements about the dotted square built on the diagonal of a square.
options: Its side is equal to the diagonal of the original square
Its area is exactly twice the area of the original square
Its perimeter is exactly twice the perimeter of the original
It is made up of 3 of the small congruent triangles
questions.explanation: The side is the diagonal and the area doubles. The perimeter grows only √2 times (not 2 times), and the dotted square is made of 4 small triangles, not 3.

questions.question: To construct a square with half the area of a given square, the tilted inner square has its vertices at which points?
options: the midpoints of the four sides
the four corners of the big square
the centre and two opposite corners
questions.explanation: Reversing the doubling construction, the smaller tilted square has its corners at the midpoints of the sides of the larger square, giving exactly half the area.

questions.question: A square has half the sidelength of another square. What fraction of the bigger square's area does it have?
questions.explanation: Halving the side halves both length and width, so the area becomes ½ × ½ = ¼. This is why the half-side square is NOT the half-area square.

questions.question: How many squares of half the sidelength are needed to fill the original square completely?
questions.explanation: Each half-side square has one quarter of the area, so four of them fill the original square.

questions.question: Halving a square is described as 'reversing' the doubling construction because:
options: the outer square's side equals the inner square's diagonal
the inner square's side equals the outer square's diagonal
the inner square has the same perimeter as the outer one
the inner square is turned through a full 90 degrees
questions.explanation: In doubling, the big square is built on the small square's diagonal. In halving we go backwards: the given (outer) square has a side equal to the diagonal of the required inner square, which is tilted 45°, not 90°.

questions.question: A square of side 10 units has a tilted square drawn inside with vertices at the midpoints of its sides. What is the area of the tilted square?
questions.explanation: The midpoint square has half the area: 100 ÷ 2 = 50 sq units. 25 would be a square of side 5 (half the side, quarter the area).

questions.question: The chapter asks you to prove that the folded figure PQRS is a square with half the area. Which approach does it suggest?
options: measure every side and angle with a ruler and a protractor
note that paper folds always produce perfect right angles
join QS and PR, find the angles formed, then use triangle congruence
apply the rectangle area formula directly to PQRS first
questions.explanation: The text says: explain by connecting QS and PR, finding the different angles formed, and then using triangle congruence. Measuring is not a proof.

questions.question: A square whose side is half the original side has half the original area.
questions.explanation: False. It has one quarter of the area, because both dimensions are halved. The half-area square is the tilted one through the midpoints.

questions.question: When the four corners of a square paper are folded inward along creases through the midpoints of the sides, the inner square PQRS has exactly half the area of the paper.
questions.explanation: True. The four folded corner triangles together cover PQRS exactly, so PQRS is half the paper's area.

questions.question: A square has side 8 units. Select ALL squares that have exactly HALF its area.
options: The square whose vertices are the midpoints of its sides
questions.explanation: Half of 64 is 32, so a square of side √32 works, and the midpoint (tilted) square has area 32 too. Side 4 gives 16 (a quarter) and side 6 gives 36.

questions.question: In a right triangle, the side opposite the right angle is called the:
questions.explanation: By definition the hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle; the other two sides are the perpendicular sides (legs).

questions.question: For the isosceles right triangle with legs 1, the text says Area of REST = 2 × Area of PEAR. Why?
options: REST is the square built on the diagonal of the square PEAR
REST has sides exactly twice as long as those of PEAR
REST is a rectangle made of two copies of PEAR
PEAR is half of a square whose side is 2 units
questions.explanation: PEAR is the unit square and REST is the square on its diagonal (the hypotenuse), so by the doubling result REST has twice the area: 2 sq units.

questions.question: If the square on the hypotenuse has area 2 sq units, so that c² = 2, the hypotenuse c equals:
questions.explanation: A square of area c² = 2 has side c = √2. √4 would be 2, and 2² is 4.

questions.question: Using c² = 2a², the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle with equal sides 5 units is:
questions.explanation: c² = 2 × 5² = 2 × 25 = 50, so c = √50 (about 7.07). √10 forgets to square 5; 10 doubles the side instead.

questions.question: Example 1: an isosceles right triangle has equal sides 12. Its hypotenuse √288 lies between which two whole numbers?
Example 2: the hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle is √72. Each of the other two sides is:
questions.explanation: c² = 2a² gives 72 = 2a², so a² = 36 and a = 6. Answering 36 stops at a² instead of taking the square root.

questions.question: The hypotenuse of an isosceles right triangle is 10. What is the length of each of the other two sides?
questions.explanation: 100 = 2a² gives a² = 50 and a = √50 ≈ 7.07 (7² = 49 < 50 < 64 = 8²). Dividing 10 by 2 or doubling 100 are the common slips.

questions.question: The equal sides of an isosceles right triangle are 3 units. Between which bounds (one decimal place) does the hypotenuse lie?
The equal sides of an isosceles right triangle are 4 units. The hypotenuse √32 lies between:
questions.explanation: 5.6² = 31.36 and 5.7² = 32.49, and 31.36 < 32 < 32.49. (8 would be the answer if you wrongly doubled the side.)

questions.question: The equal sides of an isosceles right triangle are 8 units. The hypotenuse √128 lies between:
An isosceles right triangle has equal sides 9 units. Which statement about its hypotenuse is NOT correct?
questions.explanation: c² = 2 × 81 = 162, so c = √162 = 9√2 ≈ 12.73 (12.7² = 161.29, 12.8² = 163.84). It is not 18 — doubling the side is the classic slip.

questions.question: In an isosceles right triangle with equal sides a, the hypotenuse is a√2.
questions.explanation: True. From c² = 2a² we get c = a√2, as the chapter summary states.

questions.question: If the equal sides of an isosceles right triangle are doubled, the hypotenuse becomes four times as long.
questions.explanation: False. c = a√2 is proportional to a, so doubling a doubles c. It is the AREA of the square on the hypotenuse that becomes four times.

questions.question: An isosceles right triangle has equal sides 10 units. Select ALL the correct statements.
options: Its hypotenuse lies between 14 and 15 units
The square on its hypotenuse has area 100 sq units
questions.explanation: c² = 2 × 100 = 200, so c = √200 ≈ 14.14 (14² = 196 < 200 < 225 = 15²). It is not 20, and the square on the hypotenuse has area 200, not 100.

questions.question: Since 1 < √2 < 2, the chapter calls 1 and 2 respectively:
options: an upper bound and a lower bound
an inner bound and an outer bound
a least value and a greatest value
a lower bound and an upper bound
questions.explanation: A number below √2 is a lower bound and a number above it is an upper bound. The chapter then tightens these bounds step by step.

questions.question: From 1.4² = 1.96 and 1.5² = 2.25 we can conclude that:
questions.explanation: Because 1.96 < 2 < 2.25, the side whose square is 2 lies between 1.4 and 1.5. The bounds are the sides, not their squares, and we cannot pin √2 to 1.45 from this.

questions.question: Given 1.414² = 1.999396 and 1.415² = 2.002225, the correct conclusion is:
questions.explanation: 1.999396 < 2 < 2.002225, so √2 lies between 1.414 and 1.415 — the bounds quoted in the chapter summary.

questions.question: Why can no terminating decimal starting 1.414… have a square exactly equal to 2?
options: its non-zero last digit makes the square's last decimal digit non-zero
a terminating decimal is always smaller than its own square
a terminating decimal cannot be multiplied by itself exactly
the square of such a decimal always ends in the digit 5 or 6
questions.explanation: A terminating decimal has a non-zero last digit, so its square also has a non-zero last digit after the decimal point — it can never be 2.000…. Hence √2 is non-terminating.

questions.question: In Euclid's proof, the equation 2n² = m² is impossible because the prime 2 appears:
options: an even number of times on both sides of it
an odd number of times on the left, even on the right
an odd number of times on both sides of it
an even number of times on the left, odd on the right
questions.explanation: In a square number every prime occurs an even number of times. Multiplying n² by 2 makes the count of 2s odd on the left, while m² has an even count — a contradiction.

questions.question: Euclid's book Elements, which contains the proof that √2 is not a fraction, dates from about:
questions.explanation: The chapter dates Euclid's Elements to c. 300 BCE. 800 BCE is Baudhāyana and 500 BCE is Pythagoras.

questions.question: Which statement about √2 is NOT correct?
options: it cannot be written as m/n with counting numbers m, n
its decimal expansion never comes to an end
it can be written exactly as the fraction 1414/1000
questions.explanation: 1414/1000 = 1.414 is only a lower bound (1.414² = 1.999396 ≠ 2). √2 has no fraction form and a non-terminating decimal expansion.

questions.question: Suppose √2 = m/n for counting numbers m and n. Squaring both sides and clearing the denominator gives:
questions.explanation: √2 = m/n ⇒ 2 = m²/n² ⇒ 2n² = m². This is the equation whose prime-2 count leads to the contradiction.

questions.question: The decimal expansion √2 = 1.41421356… eventually stops after finitely many digits.
questions.explanation: False. The chapter shows that no terminating decimal can square to 2, so the expansion goes on forever.

questions.question: In the prime factorisation of any square number, every prime appears an even number of times.
questions.explanation: True. Squaring doubles every exponent in the factorisation, which is the key fact in Euclid's proof.

questions.question: Select ALL the pairs that are valid bounds on √2 (lower bound first).
questions.explanation: 1.4² = 1.96 < 2 < 2.25 = 1.5² and 1.41² = 1.9881 < 2 < 2.0164 = 1.42². But 1.42² is already above 2, and 1.4² = 1.96 is below 2, so the other pairs don't trap √2.

questions.question: Śulba-Sūtra Verse 1.12 says the area of the square produced by the diagonal equals:
options: the difference of the squares on the two sides
the sum of the squares on the two sides
the product of the two sides, doubled
twice the square on the longer side
questions.explanation: Baudhāyana: 'The area of the square produced by the diagonal is the sum of the areas of the squares produced by the two sides.'

questions.question: To combine squares of sides a and b into one square, Baudhāyana makes a right-angled triangle whose perpendicular sides are:
questions.explanation: The two perpendicular sides are the sidelengths of the two squares; the square on the hypotenuse then has area a² + b².

questions.question: Verse 2.1: mark a rectangular portion of the larger square using a side of the smaller square. The diagonal of this rectangle is:
options: the side of the smaller of the two squares being combined
a segment of length a + b, the two sidelengths added together
the line that cuts the larger square into equal halves
the side of the square equal to the two squares combined
questions.explanation: The rectangle has sides a and b, so its diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs a and b — the side of the combined square.

questions.question: When squares of sides a and b (a < b) are joined and the a × b rectangle is marked inside the larger square, the leftover strip of the larger square has width:
questions.explanation: The larger square has side b; removing a rectangle of width a leaves a strip of width b − a, which appears repeatedly in the figure.

questions.question: In the construction, why is every angle of the new 4-sided figure a right angle?
options: a figure with four equal sides must have four right angles
angles x and 90 − x from two congruent triangles meet at each corner
each right triangle is isosceles, so its angles are 45° each
the diagonal of a rectangle always makes a 90° angle with a side
questions.explanation: The acute angles of each congruent right triangle are x and 90° − x. At each corner of the new figure one of each meets, giving 90°. Equal sides alone would only make a rhombus.

questions.question: In the paper activity for combining two different squares, two cuts divide the joined figure into how many pieces?
questions.explanation: Two cuts make three pieces, which are rearranged into a single larger square of side c.

questions.question: Two squares have areas 9 and 16 sq units. Using Baudhāyana's method, the side of the combined square is:
questions.explanation: Sides are 3 and 4; the right triangle with legs 3 and 4 has hypotenuse 5, since 9 + 16 = 25 = 5². 25 is the area, not the side; 7 adds the sides.

questions.question: Squares of sides 6 and 8 are combined into one square by Baudhāyana's method. The area of the new square is:
questions.explanation: The new area is the sum 36 + 64 = 100 sq units (side 10). 196 = 14² wrongly adds the sides first; 48 is 6 × 8.

questions.question: Baudhāyana's method for combining squares works only when the two squares are the same size.
questions.explanation: False. Verse 1.12 gives a general method for squares of different sizes; the same-size case is just the earlier doubling construction.

questions.question: In the combining construction, the side of the new square is the hypotenuse of the right triangle whose legs are a and b.
questions.explanation: True. The new square is built on the diagonal of the a × b rectangle, i.e. the hypotenuse of the right triangle with legs a and b.

questions.question: Select ALL the pairs of squares that combine (by Baudhāyana's method) into a square of area 169 sq units.
questions.explanation: 25 + 144 = 169 both for sides 5 and 12 and for areas 25 and 144. Sides 10 and 3 give 109, and areas 100 + 60 = 160.

questions.question: Baudhāyana's Theorem on right-angled triangles states that if c is the hypotenuse, then:
questions.explanation: The theorem says the squares on the two shorter sides add up to the square on the hypotenuse: a² + b² = c².

questions.question: The Greek philosopher-mathematician Pythagoras lived around:
questions.explanation: Pythagoras lived c. 500 BCE — a couple of hundred years after Baudhāyana (c. 800 BCE).

questions.question: Pythagoras is described in the chapter as:
questions.explanation: The text calls Pythagoras the Greek philosopher-mathematician who admired and studied this theorem.

questions.question: Why does the chapter use the name 'Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem'?
options: because the two mathematicians worked on it together
because Pythagoras translated Baudhāyana's Sanskrit verse
because it merges two different theorems into one statement
as a transitional name so everyone knows which theorem is meant
questions.explanation: The theorem is widely known as the Pythagorean Theorem, so the combined name signals the same theorem while crediting Baudhāyana, who stated it first.

questions.question: Which statement about the history of the theorem is NOT correct?
options: Pythagoras lived around 800 BCE, before Baudhāyana
Baudhāyana was the first to state the theorem in this generality
Pythagoras admired and studied this theorem
The theorem is also known as the Pythagorean Theorem
questions.explanation: Pythagoras lived c. 500 BCE, a couple of hundred years AFTER Baudhāyana (c. 800 BCE). The other three statements are made in the chapter.

questions.question: In a² + b² = c², the letter c must stand for:
options: the shorter of the two perpendicular sides
the side opposite the right angle
the longer of the two perpendicular sides
questions.explanation: c is the hypotenuse — the side opposite the right angle. Swapping c with a leg makes the equation false.

questions.question: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 3 cm and 4 cm. The theorem predicts its hypotenuse is exactly:
questions.explanation: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = c², so c = 5 cm — measuring the drawing gives about 5 cm, the theorem gives exactly 5 cm.

questions.question: The Baudhāyana-Pythagoras theorem applies to every triangle, not only right-angled ones.
questions.explanation: False. The relation a² + b² = c² holds for right-angled triangles, with c the hypotenuse.

questions.question: Select ALL the names the chapter uses for the same theorem about right-angled triangles.
questions.explanation: The chapter calls it Baudhāyana's Theorem, the Pythagorean Theorem and the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras Theorem. Fermat's Last Theorem is a different statement about higher powers.

questions.question: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 5 cm and 12 cm. Its hypotenuse is:
questions.explanation: 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13². Adding the sides (17) or subtracting them (7) are not the theorem.

questions.question: A right-angled triangle has a short side 8 cm and hypotenuse 17 cm. The third side is:
questions.explanation: 17² − 8² = 289 − 64 = 225 = 15². Since 17 is the hypotenuse, we subtract; 25 (adding) and 9 (17 − 8) are wrong.

questions.question: In a right triangle a = 5 and b = 7. The hypotenuse c lies between:
In a right triangle a = 8 and b = 12. The hypotenuse c lies between:
questions.explanation: c² = 64 + 144 = 208; 14² = 196 < 208 < 225 = 15². Adding the sides to get 20 is not the theorem.

questions.question: In a right triangle a = 9 and the hypotenuse c = 15. The side b equals:
questions.explanation: b² = 15² − 9² = 225 − 81 = 144, so b = 12. √306 comes from wrongly ADDING the squares.

questions.question: In a right triangle a = 1.5 and b = 3.5. What is c², the square of the hypotenuse?
A student finds the third side of a right triangle with a = 9 and c = 15 by computing √(81 + 225) = √306. What is the error?
options: squares can only be added when both of the numbers are odd
306 is not a perfect square, so the theorem cannot apply here
15 cannot be a hypotenuse because it is less than 9 + 9
with c known, the other leg's square is c² − a², not c² + a²
questions.explanation: a² + b² = c² rearranges to b² = c² − a² = 225 − 81 = 144, giving b = 12. The hypotenuse is the LARGEST side, so its square is the sum.

questions.question: A right triangle has shorter sides 3 and 4. The area of the square drawn on its hypotenuse is:
questions.explanation: The square on the hypotenuse has area 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 sq units. 49 = 7² wrongly adds the sides first.

questions.question: To construct a square with TRIPLE the area of a square of side a, which right triangle's hypotenuse should be used as the new side?
options: legs a and 2a, perpendicular to each other
legs a and a√2 (a side and the diagonal)
legs a and 3a, perpendicular to each other
legs a√2 and a√2, perpendicular to each other
questions.explanation: a² + (a√2)² = a² + 2a² = 3a². First double the square (diagonal a√2), then combine it with the original square. Legs a and 2a give 5a².

questions.question: To construct a square with FIVE times the area of a square of side a, use a right triangle with legs:
questions.explanation: a² + (2a)² = a² + 4a² = 5a². Legs 2a and 2a give 8a², and a and 4a give 17a².

questions.question: If a = 9 and c = 15 in a right triangle (c the hypotenuse), the third side is √306.
questions.explanation: False. The third side is √(225 − 81) = √144 = 12. Adding the squares is the error.

questions.question: A right triangle with shorter sides 5 and 12 has a hypotenuse of 13.
Select ALL the right triangles whose hypotenuse is exactly 13 units.
questions.explanation: 25 + 144 = 169 and 69 + 100 = 169, both 13². Legs 6, 7 give 85 and legs 3, 10 give 109 — neither is 169.

questions.question: Which of these triples appears in the list Baudhāyana gives in Śulba-Sūtra Verse 1.13?
questions.explanation: Verse 1.13 lists (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25), (12, 35, 37) and (15, 36, 39). The other three are valid triples but are not in his list.

questions.question: A Baudhāyana triple (a, b, c) is defined as:
options: three positive integers with a² + b² = c²
any three integers that can form a triangle
three positive integers with a + b = c
questions.explanation: A Baudhāyana (Pythagorean) triple is a set of positive integers that are the sidelengths of a right triangle, i.e. satisfy a² + b² = c².

questions.question: Is (30, 40, 50) a Baudhāyana triple?
options: no — only primitive triples are counted
questions.explanation: 900 + 1600 = 2500 = 50², so yes. In general (ka, kb, kc) is a triple whenever (a, b, c) is.

questions.question: How many Baudhāyana triples with all numbers ≤ 20 are multiples of (3, 4, 5)?
If (a, b, c) is a Baudhāyana triple, why is (ka, kb, kc) also one?
options: ka + kb = k(a + b) = kc, so the sum still matches
multiplying by k keeps every one of the numbers an integer
k² is always a perfect square, so it can be ignored
questions.explanation: Taking out the common factor k² and using a² + b² = c² gives (ka)² + (kb)² = (kc)². This is called a scaled version of (a, b, c).

questions.question: A Baudhāyana triple is called primitive when:
options: its three numbers are all smaller than 20
its numbers share no common factor above 1
its three numbers are all odd numbers
its three numbers include at least one prime
questions.explanation: Primitive means no common factor above 1: (3, 4, 5) is primitive, (9, 12, 15) is not because 3 divides all three.

questions.question: Which of these is a PRIMITIVE Baudhāyana triple?
questions.explanation: 5, 12 and 13 share no common factor. (9, 12, 15) and (6, 8, 10) are scaled (3, 4, 5); (15, 36, 39) is 3 × (5, 12, 13).

questions.question: How many primitive Baudhāyana triples have all three numbers ≤ 20?
(9, 12, 15) has common factor 3. Dividing gives (3, 4, 5), again a triple. Why does dividing by a common factor f always work?
options: dividing can never change whether numbers form a triple
3 is a prime number, so the division is always exact
15 ÷ 3 = 5 is odd, and odd hypotenuses always work
questions.explanation: Dividing each term by f divides every square by f², so the equation a² + b² = c² is preserved. This is why every triple is a scaled primitive triple.

questions.question: Which statement is NOT true?
options: every scaled version of (3, 4, 5) is a Baudhāyana triple
every triple with numbers ≤ 20 is a multiple of (3, 4, 5)
(9, 12, 15) is a scaled version of the triple (3, 4, 5)
questions.explanation: (5, 12, 13) and (8, 15, 17) have all numbers ≤ 20 but are not multiples of (3, 4, 5). The other three statements are correct.

questions.question: (15, 36, 39) is a primitive Baudhāyana triple.
questions.explanation: False. It satisfies 225 + 1296 = 1521 = 39², but all three numbers are divisible by 3 — it is 3 × (5, 12, 13), so it is not primitive.

questions.question: A scaled version (ka, kb, kc) of a primitive triple, with k > 1, is never itself primitive.
questions.explanation: True. All three terms share the common factor k > 1, so the scaled triple is not primitive.

questions.question: Select ALL the Baudhāyana triples.
The sum of the first n odd numbers, 1 + 3 + 5 + … + (2n − 1), equals:
questions.explanation: 1 = 1², 1 + 3 = 2², 1 + 3 + 5 = 3², and so on: the sum of the first n odd numbers is n².

questions.question: The nth odd number is:
questions.explanation: The odd numbers 1, 3, 5, … are 2 × 1 − 1, 2 × 2 − 1, 2 × 3 − 1, …, so the nth is 2n − 1.

questions.question: Splitting the sum of the first n odd numbers into the first (n − 1) plus the nth gives the identity:
questions.explanation: (n − 1)² is the sum of the first n − 1 odd numbers and 2n − 1 is the nth, so together they make n². Expanding (n − 1)² + 2n − 1 also gives n².

questions.question: 9 is an odd square and is the 5th odd number (9 = 2 × 5 − 1). The Baudhāyana triple this produces is:
25 is an odd square and the 13th odd number. Using (n − 1)² + (2n − 1) = n² with n = 13 gives the triple:
Apply the odd-number method to the odd square 49. Which triple results?
Apply the odd-number method to the odd square 81. Which triple results?
Continuing the pattern, the odd square 225 = 15² produces which Baudhāyana triple?
Why does the odd-number method never produce a NON-primitive triple?
options: a leg and hypotenuse differ by 1, so share no common factor
the shorter leg produced is always an odd prime number
the hypotenuse produced is always an odd prime number
two different square numbers never share a common factor
questions.explanation: The triples are (m, n − 1, n): consecutive integers n − 1 and n have no common factor above 1, so the triple is always primitive.

questions.question: Which PRIMITIVE triple can NOT be produced by the odd-number method?
questions.explanation: The method always gives a hypotenuse one more than a leg. In (8, 15, 17) the difference is 2, so it cannot arise this way — an example that the method misses some primitive triples.

questions.question: Every primitive Baudhāyana triple can be produced by the odd-square method.
questions.explanation: False. (8, 15, 17) and (20, 21, 29) are primitive, but their hypotenuse is not one more than a leg, so the method cannot produce them.

questions.question: Select ALL the odd numbers that are perfect squares and so give a Baudhāyana triple by the chapter's method.
questions.explanation: 25 = 5² gives (5, 12, 13) and 49 = 7² gives (7, 24, 25). 27 and 35 are odd but not squares, so the two parts would not both be squares.

questions.question: Fermat, who was inspired by Baudhāyana triples, was a:
options: Greek mathematician of the 3rd century BCE
questions.explanation: The chapter describes Fermat as the great French mathematician who lived during the 17th century.

questions.question: Fermat's Last Theorem says the equation xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ has no natural-number solutions when:
questions.explanation: For n = 2 there are infinitely many solutions (the Baudhāyana triples); Fermat claimed there are none for powers greater than 2.

questions.question: What observation made Fermat wonder about higher powers?
options: Euclid's proof that √2 is not a fraction
infinitely many squares are sums of two squares
the paper construction for halving a square
questions.explanation: Seeing infinitely many square numbers that are sums of two squares, Fermat asked whether a cube could be a sum of two cubes, a fourth power of two fourth powers, and so on.

questions.question: In the margin of a book Fermat wrote that he had 'a truly marvellous proof' but the margin was too small to contain it. What did he claim?
options: that the statement was actually false for most powers
that Euclid had already proved it in the Elements
that he had a proof but no room to write it down
that a proof would take about 300 more years
questions.explanation: Fermat claimed to have a proof but never wrote it down; nobody ever found it, which is why the statement became famous as Fermat's Last Theorem.

questions.question: Who finally proved Fermat's Last Theorem, and in which year?
questions.explanation: Andrew Wiles proved it in 1994. In 1963 he was a 10-year-old reading Eric Bell's book The Last Problem about the theorem.

questions.question: Which statement about Fermat's Last Theorem is NOT correct?
options: Fermat's own proof was never found
x³ + y³ = z³ has solutions in natural numbers
attempts to prove the theorem failed for over 300 years
x² + y² = z² has infinitely many natural-number solutions
questions.explanation: Fermat's Last Theorem says no perfect cube is a sum of two perfect cubes. For squares there are infinitely many solutions (the triples).

questions.question: There is a perfect cube that can be written as the sum of two perfect cubes of natural numbers.
questions.explanation: False. This is exactly the n = 3 case of Fermat's Last Theorem, proved by Wiles in 1994.

questions.question: Fermat's Last Theorem was proved roughly 30 years after Andrew Wiles first read about it as a boy.
questions.explanation: True. He read about it in 1963 and proved it in 1994 — 31 years later.

questions.question: Select ALL the equations that DO have solutions in natural numbers.
questions.explanation: Squares and first powers have plenty of solutions. By Fermat's Last Theorem, no solutions exist for any power n > 2, including cubes and fourth powers.

questions.question: The lotus-in-the-lake problem comes from the Līlāvatī, written by:
questions.explanation: The chapter translates a problem from Bhāskarāchārya's (Bhāskara II) Līlāvatī about a lotus in a lake with chakra and krauñcha birds.

questions.question: In the lotus problem, with x the depth of the lake, the right triangle formed has sides:
questions.explanation: The stem is x + 1 long (1 unit above water). Upright it is a leg of length x; swayed it is the hypotenuse x + 1; the tip moves 3 units, the other leg.

questions.question: The lotus equation 9 + x² = x² + 2x + 1 simplifies to:
questions.explanation: Subtracting x² from both sides leaves 9 = 2x + 1, so 2x = 8 and x = 4.

questions.question: What is the depth of the lake in the Līlāvatī lotus problem?
questions.explanation: From 9 = 2x + 1 we get x = 4. The tip moved 3 units and the whole stem is 5 units.

questions.question: In the lotus problem, what is the total length of the lotus stem?
questions.explanation: The stem is x + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5 units — the hypotenuse of the 3, 4, 5 triangle. 4 is only the part under water.

questions.question: Which 'very reasonable' assumption makes the lotus problem solvable by the theorem?
options: the lake has a perfectly flat circular shape
the wind pushes the stem exactly 1 unit sideways
the lotus flower floats freely on the surface
the upright stem is perpendicular to the water surface
questions.explanation: Assuming the stem is perpendicular to the water in its first position gives a right angle, so the sides 3, x, x + 1 form a right triangle.

questions.question: The diagonal of a square with sidelength 5 cm is:
questions.explanation: The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 5 and 5: √(25 + 25) = √50 ≈ 7.07 cm (between 7 and 8).

questions.question: A rhombus has diagonals of length 24 and 70 units. Its sidelength is:
questions.explanation: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles, giving legs 12 and 35: √(144 + 1225) = √1369 = 37. Using the full diagonals gives √5476 = 74 — the common slip.

questions.question: Why must the hypotenuse be the longest side of a right triangle?
options: it is always the side opposite the smallest angle
a slanted line is always longer than a level one
c² = a² + b² exceeds both a² and b², so c exceeds a and b
the triangle inequality says a + b is more than c
questions.explanation: Since a² and b² are positive, c² = a² + b² > a² and > b², hence c > a and c > b. It is opposite the LARGEST angle (the right angle).

questions.question: A right triangle has one leg 40 and hypotenuse 41. The other leg is:
questions.explanation: 41² − 40² = 1681 − 1600 = 81 = 9². √3281 adds the squares, and 81 forgets the square root.

questions.question: In the lotus problem, the depth of the lake equals the 3 units the tip of the stem moves sideways.
questions.explanation: False. The 3 units is one leg; solving 3² + x² = (x + 1)² gives a depth of 4 units.

questions.question: A rhombus whose diagonals are 24 and 70 has sides of length 37.
questions.explanation: True. Half-diagonals 12 and 35 form a right triangle with hypotenuse 37 (144 + 1225 = 1369).

questions.question: Select ALL the rectangles whose sides AND diagonal are all whole numbers.
questions.explanation: 3-4 gives diagonal 5 and 5-12 gives 13. 4 by 5 has diagonal √41 and 6 by 7 has √85 — not whole numbers.

questions.question: A square has area equal to the DIFFERENCE of the areas of squares with sides 5 and 7. Its side is:
questions.explanation: 49 − 25 = 24, so the side is √24 ≈ 4.9. Subtracting the sides (2) or adding the squares (√74) are the usual slips.

questions.question: Using the dots of a grid as vertices, a square of area 2 sq units can be made by:
options: taking the diagonal of a 1 × 1 cell as its side
taking the diagonal of a 1 × 2 rectangle as its side
taking a side of length 2 along the grid lines
joining the centres of four neighbouring cells
questions.explanation: The diagonal of a unit cell has length √2, so the tilted square on it has area 2. A 1 × 2 diagonal gives area 5 and a side of 2 gives area 4.

questions.question: Can a square of area 3 sq units be drawn with its vertices on grid dots?
options: yes — use the diagonal of a 1 × 2 rectangle
no — 3 is not a sum of two square numbers
yes — a 1 × 3 rectangle has area exactly 3
yes — join dots that are exactly √3 apart
questions.explanation: A segment between grid dots has squared length a² + b² for whole numbers a, b. The only such values near 3 are 1, 2, 4, 5 — never 3, so no such square exists.

questions.question: On a grid extending indefinitely, the possible integer areas of squares with vertices on dots are exactly:
options: every positive whole number without exception
the numbers of the form a² + b² with whole a and b
questions.explanation: A side joining two dots has squared length a² + b², and that squared length IS the area. So areas like 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10 occur but 3, 6, 7 do not.

questions.question: Which of these areas can NOT be made by a square with vertices on grid dots?
questions.explanation: 5 = 1 + 4, 8 = 4 + 4 and 10 = 1 + 9 are sums of two squares, but 6 is not, so no grid square has area 6.

questions.question: In an equilateral triangle of side 6, the altitude bisects the opposite side. The square of the height is therefore:
questions.explanation: The altitude makes a right triangle with hypotenuse 6 and base 3 (half of 6), so height² = 6² − 3² = 36 − 9 = 27.

questions.question: The area of an equilateral triangle with side 6 units is:
questions.explanation: Height = √27 ≈ 5.2, so area = ½ × 6 × √27 = 3√27 ≈ 15.6. '18' wrongly uses 6 as the height.

questions.question: Three boxes of red, blue and green balls are each labelled WRONGLY. How many boxes must you open to fix every label?
questions.explanation: Opening one box reveals its colour; since no label is correct, the remaining two colours can be placed by elimination. So one box is enough.

questions.question: In the boxes puzzle you open the box labelled RED and find BLUE balls. What is in the box labelled BLUE?
questions.explanation: Blue is now placed. The GREEN-labelled box cannot hold green (wrong label) or blue (taken), so it holds red; the BLUE-labelled box must then hold green.

questions.question: A square of area 4 sq units can be drawn on a dot grid with its sides along the grid lines.
questions.explanation: True. A 2 × 2 square has area 4; it is one of the areas (a perfect square) that sits squarely on the grid.

questions.question: Select ALL the areas that CAN be made by a square whose vertices are grid dots.
questions.explanation: 8 = 2² + 2² and 10 = 1² + 3² are sums of two squares, so both are possible; 7 and 12 are not sums of two squares.
